title: Request for a Fin Root Inspection Relief Following Repeated Findings on High-Cycle Aircraft
abstract: Operator asks for relief from a repeat fin root inspection that now drives an extra tail dock visit on its oldest short-sector aircraft, after four findings in two years at the same lateral load introduction.

sections.request: Our oldest aircraft fly six and seven sectors a day and they are reaching the point where the fin root inspection is the thing that decides how often the tail dock is used. In the last two years four of our aircraft have come out of that inspection with a finding at the same place low down on the fin, and each time we have gone into an unplanned repair with the rudder off. The inspection itself is not the problem, it is the fact that we now have to do it more often than the rest of the check package wants, so the aircraft goes into the dock for the fin and nothing else. We would like an engineering solution that puts the inspection back on the same interval as the rest of the structure, even if it costs us a heavier tail.
sections.background: The four findings were at 47000, 51000, 51500 and 53000 flight cycles on aircraft delivered between 1999 and 2003. Two were repaired under a temporary scheme that has its own repeat inspection at 3000 cycles, which has made the problem worse rather than better. Our high-cycle aircraft are averaging 2900 cycles a year on a network of forty to fifty minute sectors, and we do not plan to retire any of them before 2033. The type certificate holder has already been notified of each finding through the normal reporting channel.
sections.expected_outcome: A permanent reinforcement that restores the original inspection interval for the fin root region, that can be embodied in a single tail dock visit with the rudder removed, and that does not require the aircraft to be jacked. A published position on the two aircraft that already carry the temporary repair is also needed.

type_data.business_justification: Each unplanned tail dock visit costs the operator eleven days of aircraft availability and roughly 480 thousand euros. Four events in two years, plus a repeat inspection at 3000 cycles on the two repaired aircraft, has turned a scheduled item into the pacing constraint for the whole check programme on twenty-three aircraft.
